short: Money a federal agency transfers to an outside body to carry out a public purpose set in law, without expecting to be closely involved in the work.
definition: An award of money, or of another thing of value, that a federal agency transfers to an outside body to carry out a public purpose of support or stimulation that a law authorises [1851](#cite:1851). Under 31 U.S.C. 6304 an agency uses a grant agreement when substantial involvement between the agency and the recipient is not expected while the work is carried out; where it is expected, the instrument is a cooperative agreement [1851](#cite:1851). A newcomer may picture money handed to a person, yet at NSF an organisation submits the proposal and an unaffiliated individual is not eligible for direct funding [156](#cite:156). A rule OMB proposed on May 29, 2026, which is not final, would remove fixed amount awards as a form of grant [1803](#cite:1803).

short: An award like a grant, except that the agency expects to be substantially involved in the work while it is carried out.
definition: An instrument that transfers a thing of value to carry out a public purpose authorised by law, as a grant does, and that an agency uses under 31 U.S.C. 6305 when substantial involvement is expected between it and the recipient during the work [1851](#cite:1851). The statute does not define that involvement, and Appendix I to 2 CFR part 200 requires the funding notice to describe what the agency expects [1848](#cite:1848). A pass-through entity may also be the substantially involved party [1799](#cite:1799). At NIH these awards carry U codes, such as the U01, and each notice names the roles of NIH staff and a dispute panel [116](#cite:116). One NIAID notice puts it this way: "After award, NIH scientific or program staff will assist, guide, coordinate, or participate in project activities." [116](#cite:116)

short: The instrument an agency uses to buy property or services for the Government's own use. It is not a grant, and this guide does not cover it.
definition: The legal instrument a federal agency uses when the principal purpose of a transaction is to acquire property or services for the direct benefit or use of the United States Government, under 31 U.S.C. 6303 [1851](#cite:1851). It is one of three instruments that federal law gives an agency, beside the grant and the cooperative agreement, and the choice among them follows from the purpose of the transaction [1851](#cite:1851). 2 CFR 200.201 requires the agency or pass-through entity to decide on the instrument under these sections [1807](#cite:1807). Contracts under the Federal Acquisition Regulation are outside this guide [1851](#cite:1851). One announcement can still lead to either kind of instrument: ONR's long-range broad agency announcement lists procurement contracts, grants, cooperative agreements and other transaction agreements [334](#cite:334).

short: The federal term for grants, cooperative agreements and other aid given to carry out a public purpose, as distinct from the Government buying something for itself.
definition: What a federal agency gives when it transfers money, or another thing of value, to an outside body to carry out a public purpose that a law authorises, as against buying property or services for the Government's own use [1851](#cite:1851). The grant agreement and the cooperative agreement are the two instruments the Federal Grant and Cooperative Agreement Act provides for such a transfer [1851](#cite:1851). Subparts A and B of the Uniform Guidance apply to all federal financial assistance, and its audit subpart also reaches loans and other assistance under the Single Audit Act [1805](#cite:1805). The Grants.gov glossary describes the Assistance Listings as covering programmes that provide grants, loans, scholarships, insurance and other assistance [1880](#cite:1880). An organisation needs an active SAM.gov entity registration before it applies for such assistance as a prime awardee [1897](#cite:1897) [1899](#cite:1899). OMB's proposed rule of May 29, 2026 is titled "Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance"; it is not final, and Public Law 119-103 bars a rule arising from it through December 11, 2026 [1858](#cite:1858) [1480](#cite:1480).

short: A grant for which the agency selects the recipient, through a competition or on the merit of proposals, and decides the amount.
definition: An award for which the agency may select the recipient from among all eligible applicants, may decide whether to make an award on the content of an application, and decides the amount [1880](#cite:1880). 2 CFR 200.1 defines it as one in which the agency, under statutory authority to exercise judgment, selects the recipient or the amount through a competitive process or on the merit of proposals [1894](#cite:1894). This is the money announced in notices of funding opportunity: the notice rules in 2 CFR 200.204 apply to discretionary funding opportunities [1800](#cite:1800). Each Assistance Listing states whether a programme's awards are discretionary or non-discretionary [1808](#cite:1808). Executive Order 14332, signed August 7, 2025, applies to discretionary grants only, and under it a senior appointee reviews new funding opportunity announcements and discretionary grants [246](#cite:246).

short: Federal money that a law divides among states, territories or local governments by a set formula, with no competition among applicants.
definition: An allocation of federal funding to states, territories or local units of government, set by a distribution formula in the authorising law and regulations [1880](#cite:1880). For a mandatory grant the authorising statute requires an award to each eligible entity in the amount or by the formula it sets [1880](#cite:1880). The Uniform Guidance's own term is non-discretionary award: one made to specific recipients under statutory, eligibility and compliance requirements, such that the agency cannot exercise judgment [1894](#cite:1894). ACL describes mandatory, or formula, grants as ongoing programmes that need no application or competition [1259](#cite:1259). The government that receives the money, not the federal agency, then funds local organisations, so a non-profit applies to that state or local body [1280](#cite:1280) [1292](#cite:1292). Older Americans Act money, for one, passes from ACL to 56 state agencies on aging, then to 618 area agencies on aging, then to local service providers [1260](#cite:1260).

short: Federal money paid to a state, territory, tribe or local government, which then funds local providers. A non-profit applies to that government, not to the federal agency.
definition: Federal money paid to a state, territory, tribe or local government, which then funds local providers [1292](#cite:1292) [1259](#cite:1259). The two SAMHSA block grants and the Title V Maternal and Child Health block grant are awarded to states and territories, and a state agency applies [1130](#cite:1130) [1219](#cite:1219) [1168](#cite:1168). HUD likewise gives no Community Development Block Grant money directly to non-profits [1292](#cite:1292). How the term differs from a formula grant is not set out in the Grants.gov glossary, which had no entry for it when read on October 4, 2026 [1880](#cite:1880). 2 CFR 200.101(e) takes block grants authorised by the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981 out of subparts C, D and E of the Uniform Guidance, except for specified provisions [1805](#cite:1805). State plans for the SAMHSA block grants are made public for comment [1219](#cite:1219). The FY 2027 President's budget, a request, proposes to consolidate the two SAMHSA block grants and State Opioid Response grants into one new block grant [535](#cite:535).

short: An organisation that receives a federal award and hands part of it on to another organisation as a subaward.
definition: A recipient or subrecipient that gives a subaward to another organisation to carry out part of a federal programme [1799](#cite:1799). A university that leads a multi-site project and a state that distributes a formula grant are both pass-through entities, with the same list of duties toward their subrecipients [1823](#cite:1823). Under 2 CFR 200.332 it verifies in SAM.gov that the subrecipient is not excluded, identifies the subaward with 14 data items, evaluates the subrecipient's risk of fraud and of noncompliance, monitors its activities and reviews its reports [1823](#cite:1823). It accepts a subrecipient's federally negotiated indirect cost rate, and may not require the de minimis rate of a subrecipient that has one [1823](#cite:1823) [1802](#cite:1802). OMB's proposed rule of May 29, 2026, which is not final, would revise these sections and require pass-through entities to report subawards on SAM.gov [1803](#cite:1803).

short: Part of a federal award that the recipient passes to another organisation to carry out part of the programme, with the federal terms attached.
definition: An award that a pass-through entity makes to another organisation, the subrecipient, to carry out part of a federal programme [1799](#cite:1799). The terms and conditions of the federal award flow down to it unless a section of the Uniform Guidance or the award terms say otherwise [1805](#cite:1805). The pass-through entity identifies it as a subaward and gives 14 data items, among them the federal award number, the Assistance Listing and the indirect cost rate [1823](#cite:1823). Only the first $50,000 of each subaward counts in the pass-through entity's modified total direct cost base [1799]. With the federal agency's prior written approval a recipient may make fixed amount subawards of up to $500,000; OMB's proposed rule of May 29, 2026, which is not final, would eliminate them [1824](#cite:1824) [1803](#cite:1803). Some agencies say subgrant: OVC's victim assistance money goes to states, which subgrant it to local community-based organisations and public agencies [1280](#cite:1280).

short: An organisation that receives a subaward and carries out part of a federal programme, as distinct from a contractor that sells goods or services.
definition: An organisation that receives a subaward from a pass-through entity to carry out part of a federal award, with the federal terms flowing down to it [1799](#cite:1799) [1805](#cite:1805). Under 2 CFR 200.331 the pass-through entity decides case by case whether the other party is a subrecipient or a contractor, on the substance of the relationship [1822](#cite:1822). A subrecipient determines who is eligible for assistance, has its performance measured against programme objectives and is responsible for programme requirements; a contractor sells goods or services in its normal business and is not subject to the programme's compliance requirements [1822](#cite:1822). The classification decides whether the money counts toward the single audit threshold [1845](#cite:1845). A subrecipient has a Unique Entity ID and is not required to complete full SAM.gov registration [1899](#cite:1899) [1900](#cite:1900). A non-profit funded through a state block or formula grant is a subrecipient of the state [1823](#cite:1823) [1880](#cite:1880).

short: The state body that receives a federal formula or block grant and passes it on. A local organisation applies to it, not to the federal agency.
definition: The body in a state that receives a federal formula or block grant and to which local governments and organisations turn for pass-through funding [1343](#cite:1343) [1320](#cite:1320). The name differs by programme: for Byrne JAG only the designated state administering agencies for the 56 states, territories and the District of Columbia receive the state awards [1343](#cite:1343). For the Nonprofit Security Grant Program it is the State Administrative Agency, which takes non-profits' applications, scores them and applies to FEMA, on its own earlier deadline [1320](#cite:1320). Older Americans Act money goes to 56 state agencies on aging, and the State Mental Health Authority submits for the mental health block grant [1260](#cite:1260) [1219](#cite:1219). The calendar belongs to that body, and federal pages do not always describe the local step: those for the Title V block grant do not say how a local organisation applies [1399](#cite:1399) [1168](#cite:1168).

short: The formal public announcement that a federal agency has money to award under a programme, with the rules for applying.
definition: The formal announcement that federal funding is available through a financial assistance programme [1799](#cite:1799). The Uniform Guidance fixes what a notice contains and in what order: nine sections, from Basic Information and Eligibility to Award Notices and post-award requirements, written in plain language [1848](#cite:1848). A summary of each is displayed on Grants.gov [1800](#cite:1800). 2 CFR 200.204 sets an expectation, not a requirement, that an opportunity stay open for at least 60 calendar days, and for no fewer than 30 calendar days absent exigent circumstances [1800](#cite:1800). Executive Order 14332, signed August 7, 2025, calls these notices funding opportunity announcements and has a senior appointee review new ones before they issue [246](#cite:246). In August 2026 NSF called its twelve new solicitations Notices of Funding Opportunity [192](#cite:192). OMB's proposed rule of May 29, 2026, which is not final, would require every federal funding opportunity to be posted on Grants.gov [1803](#cite:1803).

short: NSF's name for a focused funding notice that runs for a limited period and sets its own rules on who may submit and how.
definition: One of NSF's four kinds of funding opportunity, more focused than a programme description or a programme announcement [156](#cite:156). It applies for a limited period and is used when NSF departs from the generic rules of its policy guide: limiting who may submit or how many proposals, restricting indirect costs, requiring preliminary proposals, adding review criteria or requiring cost sharing [156](#cite:156) [158](#cite:158). Programme descriptions and programme announcements use the guide's generic eligibility and preparation rules and are longer lasting [156](#cite:156) [158](#cite:158). In August 2026 NSF called its twelve new solicitations Notices of Funding Opportunity [192](#cite:192). An NSF opportunity page marked "Waiting for new publication", with no upcoming due dates, belongs to a programme whose last solicitation has run out of deadlines and has not been replaced [827](#cite:827) [857](#cite:857).

short: A standing, broad NIH notice through which an investigator sends in an application on a topic of the investigator's own choosing.
definition: A standing, broad notice of funding opportunity that an applicant uses to send NIH an investigator-initiated application, one whose topic the investigator chose and NIH did not ask for [1](#cite:1) [145](#cite:145). Each is for one activity code, such as R01, R21, R03 or R15, and not every institute joins every one [1](#cite:1) [43](#cite:43). Every NIH application answers a specific notice, so an unsolicited idea still goes in through one of these [120](#cite:120). They typically use the standard due dates, with three cycles a year, and are usually reissued when they expire [1](#cite:1) [2](#cite:2). During 2025 NIH cut the number of narrow notices and leaned more on parent announcements; active funding opportunities fell from over 800 at the start of 2025 to fewer than 500 at its end [90](#cite:90) [10](#cite:10). The P01 and the R34 have none, and each institute that uses those codes issues its own notice [1](#cite:1).

short: A standing notice, used by the defence research offices among others, that invites research proposals across the whole range of an office's interests.
definition: A standing notice that invites research proposals across an office's interests and can lead to a grant, a cooperative agreement, a contract or another transaction [334](#cite:334) [323](#cite:323). The defence research offices use it: ONR's long-range announcement, the Army Research Laboratory's announcement for foundational research and DARPA's six office-wide announcements are examples [334](#cite:334) [323](#cite:323) [344](#cite:344). Under the Army Research Laboratory announcement, valid from 21 November 2022 to 20 November 2027, proposals may be submitted at any time while it is open [341](#cite:341). DARPA says its office-wide announcements exist "to enable researchers to propose ideas that may fall outside our current priorities but have potential value to national security" [344](#cite:344). NSF also uses broad agency announcements for some use-inspired research and innovation priorities [158](#cite:158).

short: A letter NSF publishes to give information, clarify policy or announce its interest in proposals or supplements on a topic.
definition: A published letter from NSF that gives information, clarifies policy, or announces the agency's interest in planning, RAPID, EAGER, RAISE or conference proposals, or in supplements, on a topic [156](#cite:156) [158](#cite:158). It is one of NSF's four kinds of funding opportunity, beside programme descriptions, programme announcements and programme solicitations [156](#cite:156). NSF's entry page says the letters advertise supplements to existing awards and NSF's interest in specific topics [158](#cite:158). The INTERN supplement, which pays for a graduate student's internship outside academia through an existing NSF award, rests on a letter posted October 8, 2020 [870](#cite:870). A letter can be archived while the policy guide still lists the request type, as with the Career-Life Balance supplement letter [846](#cite:846) [257](#cite:257).

short: The entry, with its number, that each federal assistance programme has in the public catalogue kept at SAM.gov.
definition: A programme's entry in the Assistance Listings, the public catalogue of federal assistance programmes that the General Services Administration keeps at SAM.gov [1799](#cite:1799) [1808](#cite:1808). Each programme has a listing and a number, and that number appears in the funding notice and in the award document [1800](#cite:1800) [1810](#cite:1810). A listing gives the programme's purpose and goals, whether its awards are discretionary or non-discretionary, the projected funds, the general eligibility requirements and whether single audit requirements apply [1808](#cite:1808). Under 2 CFR 200.203 an agency assigns a listing before making awards, except in exigent circumstances [1808](#cite:1808). A NIAID cooperative agreement notice, for example, carries Assistance Listing 93.855 [116](#cite:116). The label CFDA appears beside the number on some pages: CDMRP's announcement of its FY 2026 appropriation gives Assistance Listing (CFDA) 12.420 [295](#cite:295). A pass-through entity gives the listing's title and number to each subrecipient [1823](#cite:1823).

short: The identifier an agency gives to one funding notice. It appears in the notice's summary on Grants.gov.
definition: The identifier an agency assigns to a single funding notice [1800](#cite:1800). 2 CFR 200.204(a) lists it among the summary items displayed on Grants.gov, with the agency name, the opportunity title, the announcement type, the Assistance Listing number, funding details and key dates [1800](#cite:1800). It marks one notice, where the Assistance Listing number marks the programme [1800](#cite:1800) [1808](#cite:1808). Agencies each write it their own way: one of NIH's parent R01 notices is PA-25-301, the Department of Energy's FY 2027 annual notice is DE-FOA-0003665, and HRSA's FY 2027 Service Area Competition notice is HRSA-27-005 [1](#cite:1) [277](#cite:277) [1204](#cite:1204). One competition can run under several numbers: the FY 2027 MURI announcement carries one from each of three offices, N0001426SF002, W911NF26S1000 and NOFOAFRLAFOSR20260002 [325](#cite:325).

short: An agency's advance listing on Grants.gov of a notice it plans to publish, with estimated dates. It is not yet open for applications.
definition: An advance listing, posted on Grants.gov, of a funding notice an agency intends to publish; it is a statement of intent, not an open notice [1064](#cite:1064). A forecast gives estimates: one NIOSH forecast posted September 1, 2026 shows an estimated post date of November 30, 2026, an estimated application due date of January 29, 2027, the expected number of awards and the award range [1064](#cite:1064). NIH's policy statement says its notices "are forecasted on Grants.gov prior to publication" [145](#cite:145). The estimated dates can pass with no notice: a forecast for an NIH centres notice showed an estimated post date of September 24, 2025, and no posted notice was found on October 4, 2026 [1587](#cite:1587) [1586](#cite:1586). Nine forecasts from one HHS office, dating from August 2024 and July 2025, remained on Grants.gov without posting dates [1179](#cite:1179) [1185](#cite:1185).

short: A short notice sent to a funder before the application, saying that one is coming. Some notices require it and others make it optional.
definition: A short notice sent to the funder ahead of the application [412](#cite:412) [404](#cite:404). At NSF it is non-binding and lets staff gauge the size of a competition, yet where a solicitation requires one and it is missing, the full proposal is not accepted [156](#cite:156). Whether it is required varies by notice: AFRI workshop grants require one, the FY 2026 AFRI Strengthening Agricultural Systems notice set a letter of intent date of February 26, 2026 ahead of its application deadlines, and NOAA's FY 2026 RISA notice made it optional [404](#cite:404) [412](#cite:412) [434](#cite:434). PCORI makes it a gate: an applicant submits one by a fixed deadline, is notified of its status, and only then may submit a full application [599](#cite:599) [591](#cite:591). In the two FY26 CDMRP announcements read, the pre-application that starts every application is a letter of intent [330](#cite:330) [356](#cite:356).

short: A short first-stage submission that a funder reads before the full application, to invite, encourage or discourage it.
definition: A first-stage submission that the funder reads before deciding who goes on to submit in full [414](#cite:414) [471](#cite:471). The name and the force of the answer differ by funder: an NSF preliminary proposal ends either in a binding invite or not-invite decision or in an advisory encourage or discourage [156](#cite:156). In defence research the step is a white paper, a short description sent so that a programme officer can encourage or discourage a proposal; ONR limits it to 5 pages, and the Army Research Laboratory encourages but does not require one [334](#cite:334) [341](#cite:341). The DOE Office of Science takes pre-applications through PAMS, and its FY 2027 annual notice requires one for certain review panels and makes it optional otherwise [277](#cite:277). Every CDMRP application starts with a pre-application in eBRAP [330](#cite:330) [356](#cite:356). NIFA's Specialty Crop Research Initiative judges pre-applications by industry relevance [414](#cite:414).

short: A summary of a project idea, about two pages long, that NSF asks for before certain kinds of proposal so that a programme officer can judge fit.
definition: A concise summary of a project idea, sent to NSF before certain proposal types so that a programme officer can judge whether it fits [156](#cite:156) [250](#cite:250). It goes by email or through NSF's ProSPCT tool and is generally limited to two pages or 6000 characters [156](#cite:156). For RAPID, EAGER, RAISE and planning proposals the principal investigator sends one first, and in BIO the proposal may follow only once the directorate has approved submission [156](#cite:156) [251](#cite:251) [185](#cite:185). A solicitation can set a date for it: NSF 26-524 required concept outlines by November 19, 2026, ahead of a full proposal deadline of February 11, 2027 [267](#cite:267). ARPA-E's first stage has a similar name, the concept paper, and a "discourage" notice on one does not bar a full application [301](#cite:301) [302](#cite:302).

short: A competition in which the funder caps how many applications one institution may send, so the institution chooses internally first.
definition: A funding competition in which the funder caps the number of applications or nominations one institution may put forward, so that the institution chooses among its own people before the funder sees anything [1516](#cite:1516) [2174](#cite:2174). Each notice sets its own cap: NSF's Major Research Instrumentation programme allows two submissions in Track 1 and one each in Tracks 2 and 3, the NIH C06 allows one application per institution, and NASA EPSCoR R3 allows three proposals per institution [1516](#cite:1516) [1542](#cite:1542) [1573](#cite:1573). Among NSF's training programmes an organisation may send two NRT proposals per competition [828](#cite:828). Foundations use the same device for awards to people: each of 212 participating institutions puts forward one nominee for the Pew Scholars, and the institution runs an internal competition to choose that person [2174](#cite:2174) [2175](#cite:2175). Some programmes state no limit, CAREER and DURIP among them [815](#cite:815) [1563](#cite:1563).

short: The official document by which an agency makes an award. It states the amount, the dates, and the terms and conditions.
definition: The official document an agency issues to tell a recipient that an award has been made [122](#cite:122). 2 CFR 200.211 lists sixteen data items every award document carries, among them the start and end dates of the period of performance and of the budget period, the Assistance Listings number and title, and the indirect cost rate for the award [1810](#cite:1810). HRSA's Notice of Award states the budget period, the amount, the terms and conditions and the reporting requirements [1147](#cite:1147). At NIH the recipient accepts by drawing down or requesting funds, and is then bound by the NIH Grants Policy Statement unless the notice says otherwise [122](#cite:122) [118](#cite:118). Later years can change: NIH's fiscal policy for FY 2026 said non-competing continuation awards would generally be issued at the commitment level on the Notice of Award, and under the continuing resolution that opened fiscal year 2027 on October 1, 2026 NIH stated that its institutes may issue them below that level [21](#cite:21) [83](#cite:83).

term: Budget period and period of performance
short: The period of performance is the whole span of an award, from start date to end date. It is divided into budget periods, each funded in turn.
definition: The period of performance is the time between the start and end date of a federal award, and it may contain one or more budget periods [1799](#cite:1799). A budget period is the funded portion during which the recipient is authorised to incur financial obligations; NIH's policy glossary gives its length as usually 12 months [1799](#cite:1799) [106](#cite:106). Both pairs of dates are printed in the award document [1810](#cite:1810). Costs are incurred during the approved budget period, and an agency may let unobligated balances be carried forward to later ones [1831](#cite:1831) [1815](#cite:1815). Some notices say project period for the whole span: one ACF notice funds a three-year project period with three one-year budget periods [1235](#cite:1235). NIH uses competitive segment for the initial project period of an award, of up to 5 years, or each extension from a renewal award [106](#cite:106). A renewal award begins a new and distinct period of performance [1816](#cite:1816).

short: Funding for the next budget period of an award already made, issued without a new competition.
definition: An award for a further budget period of a project that is already funded, issued without a new competition [21](#cite:21) [1151](#cite:1151). HRSA's Bureau of Primary Health Care, for example, lists a Budget Period Progress Report noncompeting continuation among the funding for existing health centres [1151](#cite:1151). At NIH an annual progress report is due about 45 or about 60 days before the next budget period starts, depending on the award [1954](#cite:1954). The amount can move with appropriations: NIH said FY 2026 continuation awards would generally be issued at the commitment level on the Notice of Award, and under the continuing resolution that opened fiscal year 2027 it stated that institutes may issue them below that level [21](#cite:21) [83](#cite:83). The Indian Health Service has non-competing continuations submitted in GrantSolutions, while its new and competing continuation announcements are posted on Grants.gov [1186](#cite:1186). At HHS the Departmental Appeals Board hears a denial of a noncompeting continuation for failure to comply [1888](#cite:1888).

short: An application to carry a funded project into a further project period. It competes again for the money.
definition: An application that competes for a further project period for a project already funded [42](#cite:42). NIH says of the R01 that applications "can be renewed by competing for an additional project period" [42](#cite:42). Under 2 CFR 200.309 the start date of a renewal award begins a new and distinct period of performance [1816](#cite:1816). NIH gives it separate standard due dates: new R01 applications are due February 5, June 5 and October 5, and renewals, resubmissions and revisions March 5, July 5 and November 5 [2](#cite:2). A renewal counts toward NIH's limit of six applications per principal investigator per calendar year [12](#cite:12). At NSF, planning, RAPID and EAGER awards may be renewed only through a renewal proposal subject to full external merit review [252](#cite:252).

short: An application sent again, in revised form, after an earlier version was not funded.
definition: A proposal sent to the funder again after an earlier version was declined [258](#cite:258). Each funder sets the terms: NSF allows a declined proposal to be resubmitted only after substantial revision, and its Engineering directorate also requires that 12 months have elapsed [258](#cite:258) [166](#cite:166). NIH's standard due dates set resubmissions apart: for the R01 they are March 5, July 5 and November 5, against February 5, June 5 and October 5 for new applications [2](#cite:2). It counts toward NIH's limit of six applications per principal investigator per calendar year [12](#cite:12). An FDA notice for clinical studies of orphan products sets separate dates for resubmissions only [561](#cite:561). A foundation may cap the number, as the American Cancer Society does in allowing two resubmissions of a Research Scholar Grant [2248](#cite:2248). At NSF a principal investigator may also ask for reconsideration within 90 days of a declination [258](#cite:258).

short: Extra money added to an award that is already running, asked for by the organisation that holds the award.
definition: Additional funds added to an award that is already running [808](#cite:808). At NIH an administrative supplement is a request for more funds during a current project period; it goes in under the administrative supplement parent announcement, PA-26-001, and does not require peer review [808](#cite:808) [1](#cite:1). NIH tells the grant holder to contact the grants management and programme officials assigned to the award before submitting [808](#cite:808). Some supplements pay for a person: at NSF the REU and INTERN supplements bring an undergraduate, or a graduate student's internship, onto an existing award, and the awardee asks for the money, not the student [830](#cite:830) [870](#cite:870). NSF advertises supplements in Dear Colleague Letters [158](#cite:158). A notice can lapse while the mechanism remains: NIH's notice for re-entry supplements expired on September 9, 2025, and its supplements page, updated April 9, 2026, still names re-entry among the uses [793](#cite:793) [808](#cite:808).

short: More time to finish a funded project: the end date of the award moves later, under rules the award sets.
definition: An extension of an award's period of performance, which moves its end date later [1816](#cite:1816). Under 2 CFR 200.308 an agency may let a recipient start a one-time extension of up to 12 months on its own, with notice at least 10 calendar days before the period ends; a no-cost extension beyond that one needs the agency's prior approval [1815](#cite:1815). NSF's terms follow that pattern: a recipient may extend a grant once by up to 12 months on notice to NSF at least ten calendar days before the end date, and a further extension needs NSF approval requested at least 45 days before the end date [259](#cite:259). Each agency's terms say which approvals it has waived [1815](#cite:1815). At NSF late project reports delay no-cost extensions [1955](#cite:1955).

short: The part of a project's cost that federal funds do not pay. Also called matching.
definition: The portion of a project's costs not paid by federal funds, also called matching [1880](#cite:1880). Whether a programme requires it is stated in the funding notice, which also says so when it is not required [1848](#cite:1848). For research grants the Uniform Guidance says voluntary committed cost sharing is not expected, and an agency may not use it as a factor in merit review unless a statute or agency regulation authorises that and the notice says so [1814](#cite:1814). NSF prohibits voluntary committed cost sharing [257](#cite:257). Where it is required the terms vary: every NEA award requires a non-federal share of at least 1 to 1, and a Head Start recipient contributes 20 percent each budget period unless a waiver is approved [651](#cite:651) [652](#cite:652) [1249](#cite:1249). A contribution counts only if, among other tests, it is verifiable in the recipient's records and is not counted for any other federal award [1814](#cite:1814). OMB's proposed rule of May 29, 2026, which is not final, lists a revision to the section [1458](#cite:1458).

term: Community Project Funding and Congressionally Directed Spending
short: Money that Congress directs to a named recipient and project in an appropriations act. The House and the Senate each have a name for it.
definition: Money for a specific recipient, project and amount that Congress names in an appropriations act; the House calls it Community Project Funding and the Senate Congressionally Directed Spending [1667](#cite:1667) [1674](#cite:1674). An organisation cannot apply to either committee: it asks its House Member or a Senator, on that office's own deadline, and the office decides whether to submit the request [1667](#cite:1667) [1674](#cite:1674). Recipients may be state, local or tribal governments and certain eligible non-profits, and for-profit entities are excluded in both chambers [1667](#cite:1667) [1675](#cite:1675). Being named does not release the money, since the named recipient still applies to the agency [1686](#cite:1686) [1672](#cite:1672). Congress designated no such funds in FY 2025 [1680](#cite:1680) [1755](#cite:1755). FY2026 projects were enacted in four laws signed between November 12, 2025 and April 30, 2026, and FY27 requests were due to the committees between March 13 and May 7, 2026 [1677](#cite:1677) [1668](#cite:1668) [1675](#cite:1675).

short: The set of forms that make up one application to one funding notice, filled in and submitted through Grants.gov.
definition: The set of forms that makes up one application to one funding opportunity on Grants.gov [1915](#cite:1915) [1918](#cite:1918). The forms an opportunity requires are loaded into its Workspace package, where members of a team fill them in, online or as downloaded PDFs, before an Authorized Organization Representative submits it [1918](#cite:1918) [1915](#cite:1915) [1965](#cite:1965). The SF-424, the standard federal application form, comes in several sets for different kinds of applicant and programme [1918](#cite:1918). The PDFs in the Grants.gov forms repository are samples and cannot be submitted with a package [1918](#cite:1918). A package can be submitted when all required forms pass error checks, the SAM.gov registration is active and the deadline has not passed, and Grants.gov keeps submitted packages for 5 years [1965](#cite:1965) [1966](#cite:1966). NIH names its package versions: its letters of collaboration take effect in fiscal year 2027 with the Forms J application package [131](#cite:131).

short: The government-wide rules for federal grants and cooperative agreements: how an award is administered, what costs it may pay and when the recipient is audited.
definition: The government-wide set of administrative requirements, cost principles and audit requirements for federal awards, issued by the Office of Management and Budget [1799](#cite:1799) [1805](#cite:1805). It binds the federal agencies that make awards and, through the award terms, recipients and subrecipients; a federal statute or regulation governs where it conflicts with the part [1805](#cite:1805). Each agency adopts it in its own chapter of 2 CFR, as HHS does at 2 CFR 300.106 [1884](#cite:1884). The text in force is the revision published April 22, 2024 and effective October 1, 2024 [1883](#cite:1883). A proposed replacement was published May 29, 2026; under section 157 of Public Law 119-103 it may not be issued or take effect through December 11, 2026 [1458](#cite:1458) [1480](#cite:1480).

short: The numbered collection in which federal regulations are printed. A citation such as 2 CFR part 200 gives the title first and the part after it.
definition: The collection in which the regulations of federal agencies are printed, arranged in numbered titles that are divided into parts and sections [1067](#cite:1067) [1013](#cite:1013) [2103](#cite:2103). A citation gives the title first and the part after it: 2 CFR part 200 is part 200 of title 2, and 34 CFR part 662 is a Department of Education programme regulation in title 34 [2103](#cite:2103) [1013](#cite:1013). A reader meets the text in two forms. One is an annual edition, such as the one revised as of January 1, 2025 [1805](#cite:1805). The other is the eCFR, an online text that shows the date to which a title is current and the date it was last amended, and keeps a record of each change to a part [2102](#cite:2102) [2103](#cite:2103).

short: The publication in which federal rules, proposed rules, executive orders and agency notices appear, each with a citation of its own.
definition: The federal publication in which agencies' final rules, proposed rules and notices appear, along with executive orders [1883](#cite:1883) [1458](#cite:1458) [246](#cite:246) [1382](#cite:1382). A citation such as 91 FR 32198 names the page on which a document starts: that one is the proposed grants rule of May 29, 2026, which runs from page 32198 to page 32305 [1858](#cite:1858). A proposed rule printed there gives the date by which comments are due [1458](#cite:1458). Some funders announce competitions in it; the Department of Education's 2026 notices are short announcements that send the reader to the full notice elsewhere [1382](#cite:1382). Its index, kept by the Office of the Federal Register, can be searched for the rule documents that cite a given part of the CFR [2094](#cite:2094).

short: The part of the Uniform Guidance that decides what an award may pay for. A cost has to be allowable, and to be allowable it has to be reasonable and allocable.
definition: The rules in subpart E of the Uniform Guidance that decide what an award may pay for [1831](#cite:1831). A cost charged to an award has to be allowable, and to be allowable it has to be reasonable and allocable, among other tests [1831](#cite:1831). A cost is reasonable if it does not exceed what a prudent person would incur in the circumstances, and it is allocable to an award according to the relative benefits received [1832](#cite:1832) [1833](#cite:1833). Subpart E then gives rules for named items of cost: alcoholic beverages and organised fundraising are unallowable, for example [1836](#cite:1836) [1840](#cite:1840). The subpart does not apply to fixed amount awards, with limited exceptions [1805](#cite:1805). OMB's proposed rule of May 29, 2026 lists revisions to several of its sections and a new 200.477; it remains a proposal [1458](#cite:1458).

short: A cost that an award is permitted to pay under the cost principles and the award's own terms.
definition: An expense that a federal award may pay because it passes the tests in 2 CFR 200.403 [1831](#cite:1831). It must be necessary and reasonable and allocable to the award, conform to limits in the principles or the award, be treated consistently as direct or indirect, be adequately documented and be incurred in the approved budget period, among other tests [1831](#cite:1831). Some items are unallowable outright, such as alcoholic beverages and lobbying costs [1836](#cite:1836) [1841](#cite:1841). Others depend on prior written approval: special purpose equipment with a unit cost of $10,000 or more is one [1839](#cite:1839). After a termination, costs are allowable only if they result from obligations properly incurred before the effective date and not in anticipation of it, or are expressly authorised [1829](#cite:1829).

short: Costs that can be tied to one particular award, such as the salaries and supplies of the project it funds.
definition: Costs that can be identified specifically with a particular final cost objective, such as a federal award [1835](#cite:1835). Under 2 CFR 200.413 it is the association of a cost with an award that decides whether the cost is direct or indirect [1835](#cite:1835). Salaries of administrative and clerical staff may be charged directly only if the services are integral to the award, the individuals can be specifically identified with it, and the costs are not also recovered as indirect costs [1835](#cite:1835). A cost may not be charged as direct if the same kind of cost in like circumstances is treated as indirect [1831](#cite:1831). Most direct costs, among them salaries and wages, materials and supplies, and travel, form the base to which an indirect cost rate is applied [1799](#cite:1799).

short: Costs of running an organisation that serve many projects at once and cannot readily be assigned to one award. An award pays them as a percentage of its direct costs.
definition: Costs incurred for a common or joint purpose that benefit more than one cost objective and cannot readily be assigned to the award that benefits [1799](#cite:1799). At major institutions of higher education and major non-profits they are classified in two groups, Facilities and Administration, which is why they are also called F&A costs [1802](#cite:1802). An award pays them as a percentage, the indirect cost rate, applied to a base of direct costs that is normally modified total direct costs [1849](#cite:1849) [1850](#cite:1850) [1799](#cite:1799). An organisation gets its rate through a negotiated agreement with its cognizant federal agency or by electing the de minimis rate [1802](#cite:1802). The rate used for an award is printed in the award document [1810](#cite:1810). Appendix III limits the administrative categories at a university to 26% of modified total direct costs [1849](#cite:1849). Programme notices state any limit that applies to a particular programme [1802](#cite:1802).

short: The document recording the indirect cost rate that one federal agency has negotiated with an organisation on behalf of all federal agencies.
definition: The record of the rate, or rates, for indirect costs that one federal agency has negotiated with an organisation on behalf of all federal agencies [1799](#cite:1799). The agency that negotiates is the organisation's cognizant agency for indirect costs [1799](#cite:1799). Once a rate is negotiated every federal agency must accept it, unless a federal statute or regulation requires a different rate or the awarding agency approves a deviation under a published procedure [1802](#cite:1802). An organisation with an established rate submits a new proposal within six months after the close of each fiscal year, and one with a current rate may ask once for an extension of up to four years [1850](#cite:1850) [1802](#cite:1802). For a university award, the rates in effect at the time of the initial award apply for the life of each competitive segment [1849](#cite:1849). The HHS, ONR and NSF pages read state no fee [1860](#cite:1860) [1861](#cite:1861) [163](#cite:163).

short: A flat indirect cost rate that an organisation with no negotiated rate may charge without negotiating one with the government.
definition: A flat percentage at which an organisation with no current federally negotiated rate may charge indirect costs without negotiating [1802](#cite:1802). Under 2 CFR 200.414(f) it is up to 15 percent of modified total direct costs; no documentation is needed to justify it, and it may be used indefinitely [1802](#cite:1802). HRSA records that HHS raised it from 10 to 15 percent effective October 1, 2024 [529](#cite:529). Two agency texts still print the older figure: NIH's policy statement as fetched and NSF's guide as printed in 2024 give 10% [64](#cite:64) [257](#cite:257). A programme whose statute or notice sets a lower limit, such as the 8 percent HHS limit on training grants, is governed by that limit [1884](#cite:1884). This 15 percent is a different thing from the 15 percent caps that four agencies tried to place on negotiated rates in 2025 [1802](#cite:1802) [24](#cite:24).

short: The base of direct costs to which an indirect cost rate is usually applied. It leaves out equipment and several other kinds of cost.
definition: The portion of an award's direct costs to which an indirect cost rate is usually applied [1799](#cite:1799). 2 CFR 200.1 defines it as all direct salaries and wages, applicable fringe benefits, materials and supplies, services, travel, and up to the first $50,000 of each subaward [1799]. It excludes equipment, capital expenditures, charges for patient care, rental costs, tuition remission, scholarships and fellowships, participant support costs, and the portion of each subaward in excess of $50,000 [1799](#cite:1799). Equipment for this purpose is property with a useful life of more than one year and a unit cost at or above the lesser of the organisation's capitalisation level or $10,000 [1799]. The $50,000 and $10,000 figures date from the revision effective October 1, 2024 [1883](#cite:1883). Every award that uses the de minimis rate is charged on this base [1802](#cite:1802).

short: The one federal agency that reviews, negotiates and approves an organisation's indirect cost rate on behalf of all federal agencies.
definition: The single federal agency that reviews, negotiates and approves an organisation's indirect cost rate proposal on behalf of all federal agencies [1799](#cite:1799). For an institution of higher education it is HHS or the Department of Defense's Office of Naval Research, normally whichever provided more funds directly to the institution for the most recent three years, and the assignment continues for five years [1849](#cite:1849). For a non-profit it is the federal agency with the largest dollar value of awards directly funded to the organisation [1850](#cite:1850). HHS does the work through Cost Allocation Services, which takes proposals through its Indirect Cost Allocation System portal [1860](#cite:1860). NSF's Cost Analysis and Pre-Award Branch negotiates for about 100 organisations [163](#cite:163). Where a cost item needs prior approval as an indirect cost, the approval comes from this agency [1834](#cite:1834).

short: A ceiling on the indirect cost rate an award will pay, set by statute, regulation or a funder's policy, whatever rate the organisation has negotiated.
definition: A ceiling on the percentage of indirect costs an award pays, applied in place of an organisation's negotiated rate [1802](#cite:1802). An agency may use a rate other than the negotiated one only when a federal statute or regulation requires it or when it approves a deviation under a published procedure [1802](#cite:1802). HHS regulations, for example, limit indirect costs on training grants to 8% of modified total direct costs [1884](#cite:1884). In 2025 four agencies announced that they would pay universities 15 percent in place of negotiated rates: NIH, DOE, NSF and the Department of Defense [24](#cite:24) [1852](#cite:1852) [237](#cite:237) [1855](#cite:1855). Each policy was set aside by the District of Massachusetts, and none was in effect on October 4, 2026 [24](#cite:24) [237](#cite:237) [289](#cite:289) [1855](#cite:1855). Appropriations conditions on indirect cost rates continue under Public Law 119-103 through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480). NIH's FY 2027 budget request proposes a 15 percent cap on F&A costs; it is a request [57](#cite:57). Foundations set limits of their own, often a flat percentage of direct costs and sometimes nothing [2120](#cite:2120) [2133](#cite:2133).

short: The audit an organisation must have for any fiscal year in which its spending of federal awards reaches a set threshold.
definition: The audit a non-federal entity must have for any fiscal year in which its spending of federal awards reaches a set amount [1845](#cite:1845). The threshold in force is $1,000,000 or more in federal awards expended during the entity's fiscal year; the Federal Audit Clearinghouse applies $750,000 to fiscal years that began before October 1, 2024 [1845](#cite:1845) [1938](#cite:1938). Money received as a subrecipient counts as federal awards expended, and payments received as a contractor do not [1845](#cite:1845). The audit is filed within 30 calendar days after the auditee receives the auditor's report or nine months after the end of the audit period, whichever is earlier [1846](#cite:1846). An entity below the threshold is exempt from federal audit requirements for that year, though its records must remain available for review [1940](#cite:1940). The requirement does not apply to for-profit organisations [1940](#cite:1940).

short: The government site, run by GSA, where an organisation files its single audit and where anyone may search the audits that have been filed.
definition: The repository of record to which an organisation submits its single audit, run by GSA's Technology Transformation Services [1881](#cite:1881) [1939](#cite:1939). An auditee uploads a PDF of the audit reporting package and submits the SF-SAC data collection form as a series of XLSX workbooks [1938](#cite:1938). Everyone who edits or certifies a submission needs a Login.gov account; credentials from the former Census Bureau clearinghouse do not work [1938](#cite:1938) [1881](#cite:1881). The site makes reporting packages public, and anyone may search filed audits [1939](#cite:1939) [1881](#cite:1881). It has a helpdesk and a list of cognizant agency contacts [1881](#cite:1881). No fee for submission is stated on the pages read [1881](#cite:1881).

short: The ending of an award, in whole or in part, before the planned end of its period of performance.
definition: The action an agency or pass-through entity takes to end an award, in whole or in part, before the planned end of the period of performance [1799](#cite:1799). 2 CFR 200.340 lists four ways: for failure to comply with the terms and conditions; with the recipient's consent; by the recipient on written notice; and under the terms of the award, including, to the extent authorised by law, if an award no longer effectuates the programme goals or agency priorities [1801](#cite:1801). Every such provision has to be stated clearly and unambiguously in the award terms [1801](#cite:1801). On July 17, 2026 the District of Massachusetts declared that the fourth ground does not allow termination based on goals or priorities identified after the award was made; it granted no vacatur or injunction [1869](#cite:1869). OMB's proposed rule of May 29, 2026 would revise the section, and no rule arising from it may take effect through December 11, 2026 [1803](#cite:1803) [1480](#cite:1480).

short: The steps that finish an award after its period of performance ends: final reports, settling of obligations and the return of money not spent.
definition: The process by which the agency or pass-through entity determines that the administrative work of an award is complete [1830](#cite:1830). It follows the end of the period of performance, including an end brought about by termination [1801](#cite:1801) [1816](#cite:1816). Under 2 CFR 200.344 a recipient submits all financial, performance and other reports, and liquidates all financial obligations, no later than 120 calendar days after the end of the period of performance; a subrecipient has 90 calendar days [1830](#cite:1830). Funds paid and not authorised to be retained are refunded promptly [1830](#cite:1830). The agency is to make every effort to finish no later than one year after the end of the period of performance, and it reports a recipient's material failure to comply in SAM.gov [1830](#cite:1830).

short: Written permission a recipient needs from the funding agency before it makes certain changes to a project or charges certain kinds of cost.
definition: Written consent that a recipient obtains from the agency before making certain changes to a funded project or charging certain kinds of cost [1815](#cite:1815) [1834](#cite:1834). Under 2 CFR 200.308 it is needed for a change in scope or objective, a change in key personnel, and disengagement of the project director for more than three months or a 25 percent reduction in time, among other changes [1815](#cite:1815). 2 CFR 200.407 lists sixteen sections under which it is a condition of a cost being allowable, among them the sections on equipment, pre-award costs and travel [1834](#cite:1834). The agency is to say within 30 days of receipt whether a requested revision is approved; the section says "should", not "must" [1815](#cite:1815). A subrecipient asks its pass-through entity [1815](#cite:1815).

short: A ceiling on the rate of salary that grant funds may pay one person, set at Executive Level II of the federal pay scale.
definition: A ceiling on the rate of salary that grant funds may pay an individual [18](#cite:18). For NIH awards Congress has set it by law at Executive Level II of the federal pay scale: $225,700 from October 1 to December 31, 2025 and $228,000 from January 1, 2026 [18](#cite:18) [20](#cite:20) [19](#cite:19) [21](#cite:21). Recipients may not draw down funds, whether direct or indirect costs, to pay salaries above the limit [18](#cite:18). Other funders use the same level. The HHS Grants Policy Statement sets a salary rate limit at Executive Level II, HRSA's application guide applies it to subrecipients as well, and a Department of Labor announcement bars its funds from paying a salary above it [528](#cite:528) [1194](#cite:1194) [1300](#cite:1300).

short: A separate budget category that, in NSF's undergraduate research programme, holds student stipends, housing and travel. It is left out of the base for indirect costs.
definition: A budget category of its own that, in NSF's Research Experiences for Undergraduates proposals, holds student stipends, housing and travel [830](#cite:830). The Uniform Guidance makes these costs allowable and requires an organisation to document how it classifies them in written policies and to treat them consistently across all federal awards [1842](#cite:1842). They are left out of modified total direct costs, the base to which an indirect cost rate is usually applied [1799](#cite:1799). NSF's REU solicitation states the point outright and prohibits recovery of indirect costs on them [830](#cite:830). Moving money from this category to another needs the agency's prior approval under 2 CFR 200.308 [1815](#cite:1815).

short: The check a federal agency makes of an applicant's finances, systems and record before it makes an award. It can end in extra conditions on the award.
definition: The assessment a federal agency makes, before an award, of the risk an applicant poses [1809](#cite:1809). Under 2 CFR 200.206 the agency checks eligibility and financial integrity information in OMB-designated databases, and keeps written procedures for an assessment that may weigh financial stability, management systems, history of performance, and audit reports and findings [1809](#cite:1809). The criteria must be described in the funding announcement [1809](#cite:1809). The review can end in specific conditions under 200.208, such as payment by reimbursement in place of advance, and the agency must remove a condition promptly once it is satisfied [1886](#cite:1886). Agencies ask for different papers: the Office of Justice Programs has applicants complete a Financial Management and System of Internal Controls Questionnaire in JustGrants [619](#cite:619). OMB's proposed rule of May 29, 2026 lists revisions to both sections [1458](#cite:1458).

short: The standard federal application form, issued in several sets for different kinds of applicant and programme and filled in through Grants.gov.
definition: The standard federal application form, issued in several sets for different kinds of applicant and programme [1918](#cite:1918). Grants.gov's forms repository divides them into families, among them the SF-424 Family, the R&R (Research and Related) Family and the SF-424 Short Organization Family [1918](#cite:1918). The forms an opportunity requires are loaded into its Workspace package; the PDFs shown in the repository are samples and cannot be submitted with an application [1915](#cite:1915) [1918](#cite:1918). Agencies call for different sets: the NEA's Part 1 application, for example, uses the Short Organization form [1934](#cite:1934). The governmentwide assurances that applicants once signed on Standard Form 424B are now made in SAM.gov when an organisation registers or renews its registration [2035](#cite:2035).

short: The standard form on which a recipient reports to the agency on the money of an award, at intervals the award sets.
definition: The standard report a recipient files with the agency on the money of an award [1820](#cite:1820). Under 2 CFR 200.328 financial reports use OMB-approved data elements such as this form, and are collected no less than annually and no more often than quarterly [1820](#cite:1820). An annual report is due no later than 90 calendar days after the reporting period, a quarterly or semiannual one no later than 30 calendar days after, and the final report no later than 120 calendar days after the period of performance [1820](#cite:1820). Each report carries a signed certification that it is true, complete and accurate [1885](#cite:1885). Where it is filed depends on the funder: recipients paid through the HHS Payment Management System file it there, and NIFA's research grantees at 1890 land-grant institutions file it through the ezFedGrants portal [1936](#cite:1936) [1961](#cite:1961) [1635](#cite:1635).

short: The government-wide standard format in which a recipient reports progress on a research award. Each agency collects it in its own system.
definition: The government-wide standard format for reporting progress on research awards [1955](#cite:1955). Each agency collects it in its own system: NIH in eRA Commons, NSF in Research.gov [1954](#cite:1954) [1955](#cite:1955). NIH has three types: annual, interim (filed with a renewal application) and final (part of closeout) [1954](#cite:1954). At NIH only the PD/PI or a delegate can start one, and only a Signing Official, or a PI the Signing Official has delegated, can submit it [1954](#cite:1954). NIH's interim and final reports are due 120 days from the end of the period of performance for the competitive segment [1954](#cite:1954). At NSF an annual project report is due no later than 90 days before the end of the current budget period [1955](#cite:1955).

short: A document in an application that says what will be done with the data a project produces: where the data will be kept, and when others may use them.
definition: A document in which an applicant says what will be done with the scientific data a project produces, including when the data will be shared and in which repositories [2029](#cite:2029). NIH's policy, in effect since January 25, 2023, applies to all NIH-funded research that generates scientific data, whatever the size of the award; training, fellowship and conference awards are among those that need no plan [124](#cite:124). NIH programme staff, not peer reviewers, assess the plan, and the approved plan becomes a term and condition of the award [124](#cite:124). NSF proposals carry a plan as well, created from April 27, 2026 with a tool in Research.gov [150](#cite:150). NIH's list of initiatives in progress, last updated September 17, 2026, includes eliminating the requirement on career development (K) awards and gives no effective date [2087](#cite:2087).

short: Federal requirements on training, disclosure and institutional safeguards that attach to research funding. People certify training; large institutions certify a programme.
definition: A group of federal requirements that attach to research funding and cover training of people and safeguards at institutions [2014](#cite:2014) [2017](#cite:2017). Section 10634 of the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 requires training for the people named on federal research and development applications, and each agency has put it into effect on its own date: NSF for all proposals from December 2, 2025, NIH for due dates on or after May 25, 2026 [33](#cite:33) [2014](#cite:2014). Each person certifies training completed within the 12 months before submission, and the organisation's authorised representative certifies as well [2014](#cite:2014) [33](#cite:33). Separately, National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 requires institutions that receive more than 50 million dollars a year in federal science and engineering support to certify that they operate a research security programme [247](#cite:247). NIH rescinded its notice on that certification on September 29, 2025 and said an implementation date had not been finalised [127](#cite:127).

short: A disclosure by each senior person on an application of their sources of support, foreign ones included, made on a government-wide form.
definition: A disclosure in which each senior/key person on an application lists sources of support, foreign ones included [247](#cite:247) [31](#cite:31). It is made on the Current and Pending (Other) Support form, one of two government-wide Common Forms written to implement NSPM-33, and the form is produced in SciENcv [249](#cite:249) [1943](#cite:1943). NIH has required the Common Forms for due dates on or after January 25, 2026, and each person, not a delegate, certifies in SciENcv that the forms are current, accurate and complete [31](#cite:31). NSF requires each person to certify the information before submission, and undisclosed current support identified later is reported within 30 calendar days [257](#cite:257) [2004](#cite:2004). From October 1, 2025 NIH recipient institutions train senior/key personnel on disclosing other support and keep a written, enforced policy [128](#cite:128).

short: A standard document about each senior person on an application, giving their appointments and affiliations. It is now a government-wide form prepared in SciENcv.
definition: A standard document about each senior/key person on an application, in which appointments and affiliations are disclosed [247](#cite:247) [31](#cite:31). It is one of the two government-wide Common Forms, the other being the Current and Pending (Other) Support form; both were written by the National Science and Technology Council Research Security Subcommittee to implement NSPM-33, with NSF as steward [249](#cite:249). The forms are produced in SciENcv, and NIH states that there is no blank template to complete outside it [1943](#cite:1943) [1942](#cite:1942). Each agency adopts them on its own date: NIH required them for due dates on or after January 25, 2026, with an NIH Biographical Sketch Supplement, and DOE for funding opportunities published on or after January 1, 2026 [31](#cite:31) [1945](#cite:1945). At NIH a person also certifies research security training through this form [33](#cite:33).

short: The federal rules for research that involves people. An institution files an assurance with the government, and a review board approves each study.
definition: The federal rules for research with people as its subjects, set out in the Common Rule, which HHS codifies at 45 CFR part 46 and twenty departments and agencies follow [1992](#cite:1992). An institution engaged in non-exempt research of this kind files a Federalwide Assurance (FWA) with the Office for Human Research Protections in HHS, a written promise to follow the rule, effective for 5 years [1986](#cite:1986) [1981](#cite:1981) [1988](#cite:1988) [1984](#cite:1984). An institutional review board (IRB) reviews and approves the research, and each such board must be registered with that office [1983](#cite:1983) [1989](#cite:1989). Federal support is given only if the institution has an assurance and, where certification is required, has certified that an IRB reviewed and approved the research [1981](#cite:1981). When several United States institutions take part in one federally supported study, they rely on one IRB [1982](#cite:1982).

short: The document in which an institution describes its animal care programme and commits to federal policy on laboratory animals. It is needed before funded animal work starts.
definition: The document in which an institution describes its animal care and use programme and commits to the Public Health Service Policy on Humane Care and Use of Laboratory Animals [1994](#cite:1994) [1999](#cite:1999). No PHS-supported activity with live vertebrate animals may be conducted until the institution has one, negotiated with the NIH Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW); OLAW's pages say the same document covers NSF- and NASA-funded animal activities [1994](#cite:1994) [1995](#cite:1995). An institution cannot apply unasked: the funding component notifies OLAW of a pending award, and OLAW then contacts the institution [1994](#cite:1994). A domestic institution needs an institutional animal care and use committee (IACUC), which has at least five members [1996](#cite:1996) [1999](#cite:1999). On how long approval lasts the sources differ: OLAW's pages say up to 4 years for Domestic and Foreign Assurances, and the PHS Policy page, as returned, says no longer than five years [1996](#cite:1996) [1998](#cite:1998) [1999](#cite:1999).

short: A statement, required for larger awards, that the applicant has made no unallowable lobbying payments and will report non-federal funds used for lobbying.
definition: A statement that a person who requests or receives a federal grant or cooperative agreement of more than $100,000 files, with a disclosure form if one is required [2039]. HHS describes it as a statement that the applicant has not made unallowable lobbying payments and will report non-federal funds used for lobbying [528]. The rule comes from 31 U.S.C. 1352 and each agency codifies it; HHS's version is 45 CFR part 93 [2039]. At NSF the governmentwide certification is made in SAM.gov [257]. The disclosure form is Standard Form LLL, Disclosure of Lobbying Activities: the Office of Justice Programs requires it if the applicant has paid or will pay anyone to lobby and the award exceeds $100,000 [619](#cite:619). A recipient collects certifications from subrecipients above $100,000 [2039](#cite:2039). Under the cost principles, lobbying costs are themselves unallowable [1841](#cite:1841).

short: NIH's governing policy guide for its grants. By accepting an award a recipient agrees to follow it unless the notice of award says otherwise.
definition: The policy guide that governs NIH grant awards [35](#cite:35). By accepting a grant award a recipient agrees to comply with its requirements unless the notice of award states otherwise [118](#cite:118). The version in force is dated March 2026; it folds in Guide notices in effect as of March 17, 2026 and supersedes the April 2024 version [98](#cite:98) [35](#cite:35). NIH continues to publish interim policy changes and clarifications as Guide notices, and a later notice can supersede the statement [98](#cite:98) [35](#cite:35). It is a separate document from the HHS Grants Policy Statement, which covers other HHS agencies and does not apply to awards made by NIH [527](#cite:527). Its section on termination lists, among other grounds, that an award no longer effectuates programme goals or agency priorities [139](#cite:139).

term: Proposal and Award Policies and Procedures Guide (PAPPG)
short: NSF's governing guide to preparing a proposal and managing an award. NSF has proposed to replace it.
definition: The guide in which NSF sets its rules for proposals and for awards [147](#cite:147) [148](#cite:148). The version in force, NSF 24-1, applies to proposals submitted or due on or after May 20, 2024, as amended by Supplement 1 for awards from December 8, 2025 and Supplement 2 for awards from January 22, 2026 [147](#cite:147) [149](#cite:149) [150](#cite:150). It has twelve chapters in two parts, the first on proposals and the second on awards [148](#cite:148). NSF grants also carry the Grant General Conditions dated July 31, 2026 [262](#cite:262). On June 24, 2026 NSF published for comment a draft Guidance on Financial Assistance to replace it; comments closed August 24, 2026, and NSF's stated goal is to issue the new guidance for use in early to mid FY2027 [152](#cite:152) [151](#cite:151).

short: A presidential order of August 7, 2025 on how federal agencies decide on and manage discretionary grants, including review by a senior appointee.
definition: A presidential order, signed August 7, 2025 and titled Improving Oversight of Federal Grantmaking, that changes how federal agencies decide on and manage discretionary grants [246](#cite:246). It has each agency head designate a senior appointee to review new funding opportunity announcements and discretionary grants for consistency with agency priorities and the national interest [246](#cite:246). It also directs the OMB Director to revise the Uniform Guidance so that discretionary grants permit termination for convenience and so that the use of grant funds for facilities and administrative costs is limited [246](#cite:246). The order creates no enforceable rights and is to be implemented consistent with applicable law [246](#cite:246). The revision it calls for was proposed on May 29, 2026 and cannot be issued or take effect through December 11, 2026 [1458](#cite:1458) [1480](#cite:1480). The Uniform Guidance in force still requires agencies to accept negotiated indirect cost rates and limits termination to the four grounds in 200.340 [1802](#cite:1802) [1801](#cite:1801).

short: The federal office that issues the government-wide rules for grants, the Uniform Guidance, which each grant-making agency then adopts.
definition: The federal office that issues the Uniform Guidance, the government-wide rules for federal awards, as 2 CFR part 200 [1799](#cite:1799) [1805](#cite:1805). The part binds the federal agencies that make awards and, through the award terms, recipients and subrecipients [1805](#cite:1805). An agency that approves a deviation from a negotiated indirect cost rate must notify this office, and agencies check applicants in databases it designates [1802](#cite:1802) [1809](#cite:1809). Financial reports use data elements it approves [1820](#cite:1820). Executive Order 14332 directs its Director to revise the Uniform Guidance, and on May 29, 2026 it published a proposed rule with the grant-making agencies as co-proposers [246](#cite:246) [1458](#cite:1458). Section 157 of Public Law 119-103 bars a rule arising from that proposal from being issued or taking effect through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480). The proposal gives its Office of Federal Financial Management as the contact [1458](#cite:1458).

short: The assessment of applications against criteria set out beforehand, usually by reviewers who know the field, before an agency decides what to fund.
definition: The assessment of applications on their merits, against stated criteria, that precedes a funding decision; some agencies say peer review [333](#cite:333) [38](#cite:38). Defense Department regulations, for example, require merit-based competitive procedures and impartial review against the criteria in the notice [333](#cite:333). NSF judges every proposal on two criteria, using ad hoc reviewers, a panel or both, while NIH, which says peer review, has two levels of it [157](#cite:157) [160](#cite:160) [38](#cite:38). Since Executive Order 14332 of August 7, 2025 a senior appointee's review of new announcements and discretionary grants sits on top of merit or peer review [246](#cite:246). A rule that OMB proposed on May 29, 2026 would describe peer review as advisory; it is a proposal and not in force [1878](#cite:1878) [2092](#cite:2092).

short: At NIH, the committee of reviewers that gives an application its first level of peer review. NIH's formal name for it is scientific review group.
definition: A committee of reviewers that carries out the first of NIH's two levels of peer review; the formal name is scientific review group, or SRG [38](#cite:38). Study sections are organised by the Center for Scientific Review and grouped by discipline into review branches [38](#cite:38) [40](#cite:40). For most research project applications with due dates from January 25, 2025, the reviewers score two factors from 1 to 9 and rate a third as sufficient or insufficient [39](#cite:39) [41](#cite:41). Under modified practices in force through the January 2027 council round, about 30-35 percent of applications are discussed, and the committee's middle third is labelled "competitive but not discussed" [16](#cite:16) [84](#cite:84) [85](#cite:85). The advisory council of the institute gives the second level of review [38](#cite:38).

short: The body of an NIH institute that gives an application its second level of review and makes funding recommendations to the institute's director.
definition: A body attached to an NIH institute or center, called a national advisory council or board, that performs the second level of peer review for research grant applications, after the study section [38](#cite:38). It makes funding recommendations to the director of the institute or center, who makes the funding decision [38](#cite:38) [15](#cite:15). NIH notices are dated by council round: the unified funding strategy took effect with the January 2026 council round, and a notice of April 15, 2026 applies from the October 2026 round forward [123](#cite:123) [16](#cite:16). After the council meets, an institute fixes the funds available, runs compliance checks and balances its portfolio, and decisions come in batches [91](#cite:91). Councils exist outside NIH as well: at NEH the National Council on the Humanities must by law review applications before the Chair decides, and SAMHSA requires National Advisory Council approval for awards over $250,000 [638](#cite:638) [1112](#cite:1112).

short: The NIH centre that receives grant applications and organises their first level of peer review in study sections.
definition: The part of NIH that organises the peer review of all NIH research proposals, cooperative agreements and research and development contracts [40](#cite:40). It receives grant applications for NIH and some other HHS components and reviews them in study sections, which are grouped into review branches by discipline [40](#cite:40). Until the change of 2025 it handled over 78% of NIH grant review, and 23 institutes and centers reviewed the other 22% [55](#cite:55). NIH announced on March 6, 2025 that all review would be centralised in CSR, which took over first-level review from the 23 institute review branches during 2025 [55](#cite:55) [54](#cite:54). An applicant may use the optional PHS Assignment Request Form to ask for assignment to a particular institute and review group [94](#cite:94) [97](#cite:97).

short: The final score that NIH peer review reports for an application as a whole. NIH proposed in August 2026 to stop reporting it.
definition: The final score that NIH peer review reports for an application as a whole, as distinct from the scores assigned reviewers give to single criteria [14](#cite:14). About half of NIH's institutes, centers and offices once funded by payline, a cut-off in these scores; from the January 2026 council round they do not, and they read the scores in the context of their priorities, strategic plans and budgets [13](#cite:13) [123](#cite:123). On August 14, 2026 NIH asked for comment on a proposal to stop reporting final overall impact scores and percentiles and to report three categories in their place [14](#cite:14). Responses were due October 13, 2026, and nothing in the proposal is in force [14](#cite:14).

short: A figure that NIH reports from peer review together with an application's final overall impact score. NIH proposed in August 2026 to stop reporting it.
definition: A figure reported from NIH peer review together with an application's final overall impact score [14](#cite:14). A notice of August 14, 2026 proposes that the two no longer be reported to applicants, institutions, programme staff, the leadership of institutes or the councils [14](#cite:14). In their place NIH would report three categories: "Most competitive" (top 25%), "Competitive" (26-50%) and "Not discussed" (over 50%) [14](#cite:14). Responses were due October 13, 2026; the notice is a request for information, and nothing in it is in force [14](#cite:14).

short: A cut-off in overall impact scores that an NIH institute used to settle which applications it would fund. NIH institutes no longer rely on paylines.
definition: A cut-off in overall impact scores that an NIH institute, center or office used to determine which applications it would fund [123](#cite:123). About half of them had used paylines before NIH adopted its unified funding strategy [13](#cite:13). From the January 2026 council round they do not rely on paylines: each funding policy follows six tenets, among them mission alignment, scientific merit, career stage and availability of funds, and each institute publishes the factors it weighs [123](#cite:123) [15](#cite:15). The National Cancer Institute, for one, states that it no longer uses paylines to choose competing grants, and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute that it has no payline or strict score cut-off [69](#cite:69) [70](#cite:70).

short: The document that gives an applicant the results of peer review of an application, at NIH and at AHRQ.
definition: The document through which an applicant receives the results of peer review; AHRQ's standing explainer, last reviewed in October 2014, describes it arriving within three months of submission [506](#cite:506). Under NIH's modified review practices, in force through the January 2027 council round, summary statements are simplified and carry no narrative paragraphs summarising the committee's discussion [16](#cite:16) [84](#cite:84). Under the proposal NIH put out for comment on August 14, 2026, written critiques and criterion scores from assigned reviewers would still be provided [14](#cite:14). NSF, for its part, releases the reviews themselves to the principal investigator with the reviewers' identities redacted [157](#cite:157).
